Circumincession
SUR-kum-in-SEH-shun
n. (Latin; theology proper; Trinitarian doctrine)
From Latin circumincessio, “mutual passage around”; from circum- (around, in a circle) + incedere (to go, to step through); the spatial metaphor suggests mutual movement through and around each other. An alternative rendering, circuminsessio (from insidere, to sit in, to dwell within), emphasizes stable mutual dwelling rather than dynamic circulation. The Greek equivalent, perichorēsis (περιχώρησις), is preferred in Eastern theology; both name the mutual indwelling of the three Persons of the Trinity.

Biblical Definition

Circumincession is the theological term for the mutual indwelling of the three Persons of the Trinity in one another — the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, with the Spirit proceeding from both and fully present in both, each Person wholly present to the others in the unity of the divine essence. Christ makes the doctrine explicit in John's Gospel: “The Father is in Me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38); “Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in Me?” (John 14:10); “that they all may be one, just as You, Father, are in Me, and I in You” (John 17:21). The mutual indwelling is not spatial but ontological: the Persons are not three containers partially or fully filled with divine substance but three distinct subsistences of the one divine essence, each fully present in and through the others. John of Damascus (d. 749) systematized the concept in Greek theology using perichorēsis; the Latin West formalized it as circumincession. Circumincession preserves two truths simultaneously: the real distinction of Persons (the Father is not the Son; the Son is not the Spirit) and the absolute unity of essence (there is one God, not three gods). Without circumincession, Trinitarian confession collapses into either modalism (the Persons are merely modes of one undifferentiated subject) or tritheism (three separate gods who happen to cooperate). Matthew 28:19 presupposes the doctrine: baptism into one name (singular) that is the Father, Son, and Spirit (three Persons) can only be coherent if those three Persons indwell one another in the unity that circumincession describes.

Webster 1828 Definition

The mutual, complete, and eternal indwelling of the three Persons of the Trinity in one another — each fully present in the others, without confusion of Persons or division of essence — the ontological ground of Trinitarian unity in diversity.

CIRCUMINCESSION, n. (Latin circumincessio). The mutual indwelling of the Persons of the Trinity: each Person is fully in the others without confusion of the Persons or division of the essence — the theological term for what Scripture calls “the Father is in Me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38).

Two complementary traditions name the same reality: perichorēsis (Greek, from perichorein, to interpenetrate) is the Eastern Patristic term used from John of Damascus onward; circumincession (Latin equivalent) is the scholastic Western term. Both name the mutual ontological presence of the Persons to one another.

Circumincession answers the question: how is the Triune God one God, not three gods, if there are truly three Persons? The Persons do not exist independently alongside each other; each subsists in and through the others. The unity of God is not the unity of a committee sharing a goal but the unity of mutual ontological indwelling without the loss of personal distinction.

John 17:21 offers an analogy for the circumincession in the believer's union with God — “that they all may be one, just as You, Father, are in Me, and I in You” — though the analogy is not identity: the union of believers is by grace through the Spirit's indwelling; the circumincession of the Persons is essential, eternal, and uncreated.

Circumincession is not speculative addition to Scripture; it is the systematic summary of what Scripture repeatedly asserts. John 10:38; 14:10-11; 17:21-23 all articulate the mutual indwelling in Christ's own words. The term gives the exegetical reality a stable conceptual anchor that guards against both modalism (no real Persons) and tritheism (no real unity).

Key Scripture

John 10:38 — "But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him."

John 14:10 — "Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works."

John 17:21 — "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me."

Matthew 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Modern Corruption

Modalism denies the real personal distinctions and makes circumincession incoherent; tritheism (including social trinitarianism) denies the essential unity and makes the Persons independent agents; open theism's relational Trinity lacks the ontological depth the doctrine requires.

expand to see more

Social trinitarianism (Jürgen Moltmann, Miroslav Volf, Cornelius Plantinga), influential in contemporary evangelical and egalitarian theology, so emphasizes the distinction of Persons that they begin to resemble three independent centers of consciousness in perfect mutual love. This position functionally abandons circumincession: if the Persons are primarily three co-equal centers of will and consciousness, the mutual indwelling of John 10:38 becomes metaphorical solidarity rather than ontological interpenetration. The resulting “Trinity” is a divine committee — a model that is theologically tritheistic even when it protests otherwise, and which cannot ground the unitary divine will that Scripture presupposes in creation, providence, and redemption. Egalitarians who use the social Trinity to argue that the Father-Son economic subordination proves no eternal authority relation exist among the Persons have imported their anthropology into their theology.

Modalism (Oneness Pentecostalism, United Pentecostal Church International) denies the real distinction of Persons and therefore makes circumincession vacuous: three names or modes of one divine Person cannot “indwell” each other in any meaningful ontological sense. But Christ's high-priestly prayer in John 17 presupposes that the Father and Son are genuinely distinct Persons who are genuinely one — the prayer is not to Himself but to Another, and the oneness He prays for has the Father-Son mutual indwelling as its model and source. Modalism cannot accommodate the prayer as real communication between real Persons; the confession of circumincession can, and does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin circumincessio (mutual going around) and circuminsessio (mutual sitting-in); Greek perichorēsis (interpenetration) from John of Damascus; the biblical anchor is Christ's own formula “the Father in Me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38; 14:10).

expand to see more

Latin circumincessio — mutual passage around; from circum- (around) + incedere (to go, to step through); the spatial metaphor suggests mutual movement through one another; preferred by scholastic Western theologians for the dynamic sense of interpenetration.

Latin circuminsessio — mutual inherence or sitting-in; alternative Latin rendering from insidere (to sit in, to dwell within); emphasizes stable mutual dwelling rather than dynamic circulation; some scholastics preferred this for its sense of rest and permanence.

Greek perichorēsis (περιχώρησις) — mutual coinherence, interpenetration; from peri- (around) + chorein (to make room, to go, to contain); used by Pseudo-Dionysius, Maximus the Confessor, and systematized by John of Damascus for Trinitarian mutual indwelling; also used for the two natures of Christ in the one Person.

Greek en (ἐν) — in; John's repeated formula “the Father in Me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38; 14:10-11; 17:21) uses the locative en for ontological indwelling; the preposition is simple but theologically decisive.

Greek monogenēs (μονογενής) — only-begotten; John 1:14, 18 uses this for the Son's unique relationship to the Father; the eternal generation of the Son is the ontological basis for why His indwelling in the Father is not the indwelling of a creature in its Creator but of One who shares the divine essence by eternal generation.

Usage

"Circumincession guards Trinitarian preaching from the two most common colloquial errors: treating the three Persons as three independent agents who agreed to work together for salvation (tritheism), or treating Father, Son, and Spirit as three masks of one divine Person (modalism)."

"The doctrine has deep pastoral implications for prayer: when we pray to the Father in the name of the Son by the Spirit (Eph 2:18), we are not navigating three separate divine offices; we are, by grace, entering the circle of mutual indwelling that the Triune God has always been."

"Preaching that dwells on the relationships among the Persons — the eternal love of the Father for the Son (John 17:24), the Spirit's procession and mission (John 15:26), the Son's intercession (Heb 7:25) — without circumincession reduces Trinitarian reflection to biography of three individuals rather than contemplation of the one God who eternally is communion."
